title: The Scotch Game
standfirst: Where the Ruy López squeezes for thirty moves, the Scotch resolves the centre immediately and gets everyone into open play. Far less theory, and much easier to understand.

steps.title: The opposite temperament
body: The Ruy López keeps the tension as long as possible. The Scotch does the reverse: it trades in the centre on move three and plays with free pieces and open lines.
If you don't enjoy manoeuvring behind a locked pawn chain, this is your opening.

steps.title: The usual start
body: Nothing new yet — the game is identical to the Italian and the Ruy for two moves.

steps.title: Strike at once
body: This is the Scotch. White challenges e5 a second time, and Black cannot defend it again — the pawn must capture or be lost.
Two pawns hitting the same square is the standard way to force matters in the centre.

steps.title: Black takes
body: Forced, in effect. The alternatives all concede more than the pawn is worth.

steps.title: The centre resolves
body: White regains the pawn with a beautifully placed knight, and the e-file is now half-open for the rook that will come to e1. Compare the Ruy: there, this tension lasts for ages. Here it lasted one move.

steps.title: Question the knight
body: Black develops with a threat, attacking the d4 knight. The knight is White's best piece, so this is the most testing reply.

steps.title: Defend it, and offer a trade
body: The bishop defends the knight and lines up against its counterpart on c5. If Black takes, White recaptures toward the centre — which is usually the right direction.

steps.title: Bring the heavy piece to bear
body: Unusual by normal opening rules — the queen comes out early — but it's the main line, because d4 needs a third attacker and there is nothing to chase her with.

steps.title: Prop it up again
body: Another defender for the knight, and a useful square-grab in the centre. The little pawn moves are doing most of the work in this opening.

steps.title: Behind the queen
body: Black's knight develops to the only sensible square, since f6 is occupied by his own queen. That awkwardness is the price of bringing her out early.
The position is balanced and open. Both sides castle next and the middlegame starts almost immediately — no memorised traps required.
